item.content:encoded:
In dressage, success is often judged over a matter of minutes.

A horse enters the arena and, for the next seven minutes, every transition, movement and aid is scrutinised. The smallest inconsistency can separate a personal best from a championship performance.

For Australian dressage riders Dave and Robbie McKinnon, creating that consistency starts long before the first salute. It begins at home, in the daily routines that shape how horses train, travel and ultimately perform.

Over the years, the McKinnons have built a reputation for developing horses across multiple levels of the sport. Their stable is rarely home to just one type of horse. 

Like many professional training operations, they also manage horses arriving from a variety of owners, often on very different feeding programs.

The challenge wasn't finding more feed products. It was finding fewer.

"We used to have a lot of horses come into training with a very large amount of feed options,” said Robbie. 

"Our feed room wasn't big enough to hold the options that we had, and we found moving to Pryde’s really helped us condense that and simplify our feeding, but still get the same nutrients, and it was really much more uncomplicated and the horses all look really great from simplifying the options," she said. 

It is a problem many horse owners can relate to. Whether managing a competition stable with dozens of horses or feeding a handful at home, nutritional programs can quickly become complicated. 

Different horses are fed different products, extra supplements accumulate, and before long the feed room begins to look complex. 

For the McKinnon’s, the answer was not adding another product to the mix. It was simplifying the entire approach.

That philosophy has paid dividends in the arena.

Recently, the team celebrated a remarkable run of results at the Australian Dressage Championships, with Lea Rian (Zimba) claiming the Australian Grand Prix Championship, MacArthur Sequoia (Simi) crowned Australian Elementary Champion, SPB Movie Magic (Movie) taking out the Australian Pony Medium Championship and SPH Fortino (Frankie) placing in the Inter II.
While championships are won through talent, training and horsemanship, Dave believes consistency has been one of the biggest advantages in their program.

"The feed that we found the best for what we do was Pryde’s EasiSport due to its low sugar, low starch elements,” said Dave. 

“It just meant that with what we do - taking horses and trying to get them to concentrate for seven minutes in a dressage test - meant that they all just stayed the same.

“There was no ‘highs and lows’, there was no fizzy behaviour.

"It got rid of all of the ‘ups and downs’, especially when we had to compete the horses and spend a week at a competition.

You see a lot of people turn up and the horses are really fresh and hot and then by the end they're really dull and (EasiSport) got rid of that and kept the horses really stable and calm and consistent for the whole event.

“For us, moving to Pryde's EasiSport was a massive advantage," he said.

For the McKinnons, it all comes back to consistency. Whether they're training at home or competing away for a week, they want horses that feel the same every day. That's why simplifying their feeding program has been such a win, proving that effective nutrition doesn't have to be complicated, no matter the size of the stable.

Looking for a simpler way to feed for performance? Discover the difference Pryde's EasiSport can make.

item.title: How can you safely add condition to a laminitis-prone horse this spring?
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au
item.description: For many horse owners, spring brings longer days and fresh green grass. However, for owners of horses and ponies with a history of laminitis, the season can also bring heightened anxiety. While horses and ponies carrying excess body condition are commonly associated with endocrinopathic laminitis, some normal-weight or underweight horses can also be at risk.
item.content:encoded:
For many horse owners, spring brings longer days and fresh green grass. However, for owners of horses and ponies with a history of laminitis, the season can also bring heightened anxiety. While horses and ponies carrying excess body condition are commonly associated with endocrinopathic laminitis, some normal-weight or underweight horses can also be at risk. This is particularly relevant in older horses with pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction (PPID), where muscle loss and declining body condition may coexist with insulin dysregulation. Not every horse with PPID has insulin dysregulation; veterinary testing helps assess individual risk.

The key is finding a feeding approach that supports safe weight gain without increasing the risk of laminitis.

Pryde's equine nutritionist Bethanie Gagliardi said many owners are surprised to learn that laminitis is not exclusively linked to obesity.

"One of the biggest misconceptions we see is that only overweight horses develop laminitis," Gagliardi said.

"In reality, horses with underlying metabolic conditions can be underweight and still be highly susceptible. The challenge is providing sufficient calories to support weight gain while carefully managing dietary sugar and starch intake."

Understanding why laminitis occurs and which feeding strategies are safest can help owners confidently navigate the high-risk spring period.

We've outlined strategies for safely feeding the underweight laminitis-prone horse.

1. Understand the underlying cause of laminitis

Insulin-associated laminitis is a common form of laminitis. Insulin dysregulation is central to equine metabolic syndrome and can also occur in horses with PPID. Relevant endocrine conditions include:

  • Equine metabolic syndrome (EMS)

  • Pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction (PPID or Cushing's disease)

Horses with insulin dysregulation may produce excessive insulin after consuming sugar and starch. Elevated insulin concentrations are a primary driver of endocrinopathic laminitis. In forage analysis, non-structural carbohydrates (NSC) commonly means water-soluble carbohydrates (WSC, including sugars and fructans) plus starch. This differs from ethanol-soluble carbohydrates (ESC) plus starch, so laboratory results and feed specifications must be compared using the same measure.

Importantly, body condition alone does not determine risk. While obesity remains a major risk factor for insulin dysregulation and laminitis, horses with PPID or other endocrine disorders may develop laminitis even when they are of normal weight or underweight.

2. Manage spring pasture carefully

Spring pasture presents one of the biggest challenges for laminitis-prone horses.

Pasture NSC concentrations vary with grass species, sunlight, temperature and plant stress. Conditions that can favour carbohydrate accumulation include:

  • Bright sunlight when growth is limited by cool temperatures

  • After sunny days followed by frosty nights

  • During periods of pasture stress, including drought, frost or overgrazing

NSC concentrations often rise during sunny days and decline overnight when conditions allow continued plant growth. However, they can remain elevated after cold or frosty nights. Rainfall or rapid growth alone does not reliably predict carbohydrate content, and early-morning grazing is not automatically safe.

To reduce risk:

  • Restrict access to high-risk pasture

  • Allow grazing in early hours of the morning, only when approved by a vet following an individual risk assessment

  • Do not rely on a fixed turnout window; some highly susceptible horses may need pasture excluded altogether

  • Monitor seasonal changes closely

3. Build the diet around low-NSC hay

Forage should form the foundation of any weight-gain program for a laminitis-prone horse.

For horses with insulin dysregulation, a conservative published recommendation is to select diet components containing no more than 10% NSC on a dry-matter basis. This is a management target, not a guarantee of suitability for every horse. A vet and equine nutritionist should interpret the carbohydrate analysis and balance sufficient calories for gradual weight gain.

For an underweight horse, the vet and nutritionist may consider approximately 2–3% of bodyweight per day as forage dry matter, adjusted to the horse's condition, intake capacity and metabolic response. This is not a universal prescription, particularly for horses with active laminitis or other health problems.

For a 500 kg horse, 2–3% of bodyweight equates to 10–15 kg of forage dry matter daily—not 10–15 kg of hay weighed as fed. Calculate the actual hay allowance using its measured dry-matter percentage and account for other forage in the ration.

Potential forage options include the following, but every hay batch should be tested; species alone does not establish suitability:

  • Rhodes grass

  • Lucerne

  • Native grass hay

  • Teff

Soaking can reduce soluble carbohydrates, but the reduction varies and soaking does not guarantee that untested hay is suitable. Use forage analysis and veterinary advice to decide whether soaking is appropriate. Lucerne is often relatively low in NSC and may provide useful calories, but its suitability also needs to be confirmed by testing.

Oaten, wheaten, barley and ryegrass hay can contain substantial NSC and are generally unsuitable for laminitis prone horses.

4. Choose a suitable low-NSC fortified concentrate feed

When additional calories are needed, selecting an appropriate concentrate feed is critical.

Look for a feed that:

  • Has a total NSC content of less than 12%

  • Is free from grain and grain by-products, such as EasiSport, while also meeting the horse's individual carbohydrate requirements

  • Provides high-quality protein sources such as soybean meal

  • Is fortified with essential vitamins and minerals

  • Supports condition gain without excessive starch intake

Owners should read both ingredient labels and nutrient analyses, even on products marketed as grain-free. A ‘grain-free’ claim does not automatically mean suitable for an insulin-dysregulated horse. Assess the finished feed's carbohydrate content, meal size and contribution to the whole ration.

It is best to avoid feeds containing grain and grain by product ingredients including:

  • Wheat

  • Barley

  • Corn

  • Oats

  • Rice

  • Triticale

  • Rye

  • Millrun

  • Millmix

  • Bran (rice or wheat)

  • Pollard

  • Middlings

5. Add appropriate calories when extra condition is needed

Some horses require additional energy beyond their forage and fortified concentrate feed allocation.

If more calories are needed, discuss oil and fibre-based options with a vet or equine nutritionist. Products to assess within the individual ration include:

  • EasiOil

  • EasiFibre, LupinPak and ProteinPak

  • EasiFibre, LupinPak and ProteinPak are not complete feeds and do not contain added vitamin-and-mineral premixes, so the overall ration must still meet vitamin and mineral requirements.  

6. Maximise forage consumption time

Healthy weight gain is not simply about how much a horse eats, but also how long it spends eating.

Extending the time spent eating forage can:

  • Reduce gorging behaviour

  • Improve digestive function

  • Support hindgut health

  • Minimise boredom and stress

  • Improve feed utilisation

  • Helpful tools include:

  • Slow feeders

  • Multiple hay nets

  • Round bale nets

  • Porta-Grazers and similar forage systems

A healthy digestive system often translates to better feed conversion and more efficient weight gain.

7. Monitor progress regularly

Successful weight gain should be gradual and measured.

Owners should:

  • Assess body condition score weekly

  • Weigh feed accurately

  • Adjust rations as necessary

  • Take regular progress photographs

  • Monitor closely for any signs of foot soreness or laminitis flare-ups

Consistent monitoring helps ensure weight is being gained safely without compromising metabolic health.

Professional Insight

According to Bethanie Gagliardi, managing the underweight laminitis-prone horse requires balancing two competing priorities: increasing calorie intake while carefully controlling sugar and starch consumption.

"The safest approach is to think fibre first. High-quality low-NSC forage should form the basis of the diet, with additional calories coming from carefully selected low-starch feeds and supplements. This is especially important in older horses with PPID, where maintaining body condition and muscle mass can be challenging while still requiring careful control of dietary sugar and starch. Rapid dietary changes or relying on spring grass for weight gain can increase the risk of a setback.

She also emphasises that every horse's requirements are different, particularly when conditions such as EMS or PPID are involved.

"Regular monitoring is essential. If a horse isn't gaining weight as expected, it's important to review the entire diet rather than simply increasing feed volume. The goal is sustainable condition gain while keeping insulin levels under control."

FAQs

1. Can an underweight horse get laminitis?

Yes. Although overweight horses are more commonly affected by endocrinopathic laminitis, horses with conditions such as PPID or insulin dysregulation can develop laminitis even when they are of normal weight or underweight.

2. Why is spring considered a high-risk period?

Spring pasture can contain elevated NSC, but concentrations depend on species, sunlight, temperature and plant stress—not rainfall or rapid growth alone. Cold or frosty nights can leave carbohydrate concentrations elevated into the morning. No fixed grazing window is safe for every susceptible horse; seek veterinary advice on whether any pasture access is appropriate.

3. What does NSC mean?

NSC stands for non-structural carbohydrates. In forage analysis, it commonly means water-soluble carbohydrates, including sugars and fructans, plus starch. It is not the same as ESC plus starch. For insulin-dysregulated horses, a conservative published target is no more than 10% NSC on a dry-matter basis, interpreted by a vet or nutritionist for the individual horse.

4. How much hay should a skinny laminitis-prone horse receive?

The allowance must be individualised. A vet and nutritionist may consider approximately 2–3% of bodyweight daily as forage dry matter for an underweight horse, adjusted for health, intake and metabolic response. For a 500 kg horse, that is 10–15 kg of forage dry matter, not hay weighed as fed. Test each hay batch, calculate the as-fed amount from its dry-matter content and account for other forage. Soaking does not guarantee that untested hay is suitable.

5. Can grain-free feeds still contain ingredients that may not be suitable?

Yes. A grain-free label alone does not establish suitability. Check the finished feed's ingredients, NSC levels, meal size and contribution to the whole ration.

6. What is the safest way to increase calories?

With veterinary and nutritional guidance, use tested low-NSC forage and carefully selected fortified concentrate feeds, oils or fibre-based supplements rather than relying on high-starch feeds. Assess each product within the whole ration; grain-free supplements are not automatically suitable or nutritionally complete.

7. How quickly should an underweight horse gain weight?

Weight gain should be gradual and monitored closely through body condition scoring, feed assessments and regular progress photos.

8. What is the most important feeding tip for these horses?

Maintain a diet that is low in sugar and starch, minimise access to high-risk pasture, and make all feed changes gradually over a period of at least two weeks.

item.title: Pryde’s EasiFeed Extends Long-Standing Partnership with Adelaide Equestrian Festival for a further three years
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au
item.description: One of the Festival’s longest-standing partnerships will continue, with Pryde’s EasiFeed signing a new exclusive agreement as the Official Feed Partner of the Adelaide Equestrian Festival and elevating their brand position to Major Partner status.
item.content:encoded:
One of the Festival’s longest-standing partnerships will continue, with Pryde’s EasiFeed signing a new exclusive agreement as the Official Feed Partner of the Adelaide Equestrian Festival and elevating their brand position to Major Partner status.

The partnership will also see Pryde’s EasiFeed aligned with the Dressage discipline across two days of competition, providing the brand with a prominent presence as competitors begin their campaign in the arena before progressing to the Cross Country and Show Jumping phases.

The partnership is one of the longest-standing commercial relationships in the Festival’s history and reflects a shared commitment to equestrian sport, horse health and performance.

Adelaide Equestrian Festival Event Director Kirsty Withers said the longevity of the partnership made the renewal particularly significant.

“Long-term partnerships like this are incredibly important to our Festival. Pryde’s has supported the event through many stages of its growth and evolution, and their continued commitment demonstrates the value they see in the Festival, our competitors and our highly engaged equestrian audience.”

The renewed partnership will see Pryde’s EasiFeed maintain a strong presence throughout the four-day Festival, connecting with competitors, horse owners and spectators through its Dressage alignment, brand activation and broader Official Feed Partner rights.

Kylie Hardy, Brand Manager – Pryde’s EasiFeed said the company was proud to continue its association with the Adelaide Equestrian Festival.

“We’re incredibly proud to continue our partnership with the Adelaide Equestrian Festival, a relationship that is now approaching two decades. For Pryde’s, this partnership has always been about more than brand presence. It’s an opportunity to support one of Australia’s most important equestrian events, connect with riders and horse owners, and be part of a Festival that showcases our sport at the very highest level.”

The Adelaide Equestrian Festival is held in the Adelaide’s East Park Lands, bringing together elite international equestrian competition and a four-day Festival experience in the heart of the city.

item.title: Steven Hart pursuing glory at Pryde’s EasiFeed Warwick Gold Cup
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au
item.description: Steven Hart has spent more than two decades chasing the Warwick Gold Cup. It is a dream he has spent much of his life chasing.
item.content:encoded:
Steven Hart has spent more than two decades chasing the Warwick Gold Cup. 

It is a dream he has spent much of his life vying for.

Steve has built his career around developing performance horses, competing at the highest level, and passing his knowledge on to the next generation.

Now, as he prepares for another Warwick Gold Cup, the ambition remains as strong as ever.

“It’d be a dream come true to win, an absolute dream come true,” Steve said.

“I’ve been dreaming of it and working towards it pretty much all my life.

“You try to make sure your horses are right, you breed your horses and train them so that you can go to the Warwick Gold Cup and be competitive.”

Steve has been making the trip to the event since around 2004, missing only a handful of editions depending on his horsepower and commitments.

He has already come close to achieving his dream, finishing third in the Warwick Gold Cup in both 2006 and 2008, along with a number of other strong final results.

“I was third in 2006 and third in 2008 and have had a bunch of other places as well over the years,” he said.

“Every time you go there, just to make a final, even to get a place, is a real thrill.”

That longevity has only reinforced what makes Warwick Cup Gold so special.

“The history and the prestige of it is so special,” he said.

“I actually grew up watching videos of it and learning about the history and the prestige of it. It’s like winning the Melbourne Cup.”

First contested in 1928 as part of Warwick’s Australian campdraft championships, the Warwick Gold Cup has grown into one of the defining events on the Australian campdrafting calendar. 

It is a test of horsemanship, stock sense, timing and the partnership between horse and rider, with competitors from across the country converging on Warwick to chase a place in the event’s history. The event has been proudly supported by Pryde’s as naming rights sponsor since 2015, building on the company’s long-standing commitment to campdrafting and the people who make the sport what it is today.

The Gold Cup attracts a deep field of experienced competitors and Steve knows there is little room for error.

“All the competitors are really good, anyone can win it,” he said.

“They’ve all set themselves and got themselves in a position where they can go and put cattle around.

“You’ve got mainstays like Ben Hall and Pete Comiskey that are very, very competitive, and then Matty Holtz as well. Pete and Matty are both Pryde’s riders.”

Steve knows that success begins well before he enters the camp.

He will campaign both Yaven Smooth Spin in the Warwick Gold Cup, and his homebred mare Hart’s Allure.

Preparation is about building confidence and making sure his horses are comfortable with the work they will be asked to do when the pressure is on.

“Just making sure they’re confident and comfortable within their exercises,” Steve said.

Nutrition plays an important role in ensuring his horses are ready to perform, with Steve taking a considered approach to the diets of both his own horses and those of his clients.

“BioMare is my mainstay,” he said.

“We also use EasiResponse, depending on the horse, and Pryde’s EasiOil, which is great for more energy but doesn’t affect their behaviour.”

Steve said Pryde’s is an important part of his program, giving him confidence that his horses are receiving the nutrition they need through training and competition.

“Pryde’s has been absolutely amazing,” he said.

“What they say is in the feed, is actually in the feed, it’s in there, and it works. The horses can digest it to use to their advantage.”

“They always look good and feel good.”

While the Gold Cup remains the ultimate competitive goal, Steve’s connection with campdrafting goes well beyond his own results.

“I’ve enjoyed doing the sport pretty much all my life,” he said.

“I grew up chasing cattle and then to be able to go into an arena and compete, plus enjoy the people and the family setting around it has been absolutely brilliant.”

And while Steve has seen plenty of change during his years around Warwick, he believes the event continues to evolve while retaining the qualities that make it special.

“This year they’ve adjusted the program so the Warwick Gold Cup final is on a Saturday, which will draw in more of the crowd.

“They’re always evolving as they go along and just making things better.”

For Steve, that evolution only adds to the appeal of an event that has been part of his life for more than two decades.

The dream remains the same.

To arrive at Warwick with the right horses, make the most of the opportunities that come his way and, ultimately, lift the Gold Cup.

After all these years, Steve is still chasing the dream.

The Pryde’s EasiFeed Warwick Gold Cup Campdraft takes place from 19-25 October at the Warwick Showgrounds in Queensland. Make sure you stop by and see how the right nutrition can make a difference to your horse's health and performance.

item.title: Jesper Barrett leads a promising junior lineup at Equimillion 2026, where Pryde’s EasiFeed is the Official Feed Partner
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au
item.description: Jesper Barrett is heading to Equimillion 2026 with three off‑the‑track Thoroughbreds and a perspective few competitors share. As a trackwork rider and stable hand, Barrett works with racehorses every day, then heads home to train his own team of retired thoroughbreds.
item.content:encoded:
Jesper Barrett is heading to Equimillion 2026 with three off‑the‑track thoroughbreds and a perspective few competitors share. As a trackwork rider and stable hand, Barrett works with racehorses every day, then heads home to train his own team of retired thoroughbreds.

For Jesper, Equimillion is more than a competition.

“Because I work in the racing industry, I’m able to see these racehorses come from the track and turn into performance horses and compete at this event. It’s a cool experience,” Barrett said.

“All the hard work they put in, it really pays off to see such great success for the thoroughbreds, and especially in the success that I’ve had with my own team of horses,” he said. 

Jesper’s connection to the breed runs deep. Each morning he’s awake before dawn, heading to the track to ride fast work for trainer Todd Howlett. His job is hands‑on and relentless.

Once his stable duties are finished, he’ll ride anywhere from four to ten racehorses a day.

“I definitely love the thoroughbreds,” he said. “I work there in the mornings and I go to a racetrack and I do fastwork, and then I come home and ride four more of my own. 

“Just working day in and day out, I just love the breed and just love the capability and space to learn and take in new information,” he said.

Jesper’s daily immersion in the racing world combined with a strong equestrian lineage - his parents, Craig and Prue Barrett, are leading coaches and former Australian representatives, while his older brother Oliver recently represented Australia at the FEI World Equestrian Championships - gives him a natural edge as he develops retired thoroughbreds in their second careers.

His Equimillion 2026 team includes Ballyhoo, Satodaze and Twenty Four Guns – each at a different stage of their off‑the‑track journey.

Ballyhoo, the 2024 junior dressage champion, returns after an 18‑month break. Barrett hopes to “pull out a great test” and replicate past success.

Satodaze, a careful jumper and bold cross‑country horse, is entered in the one‑star eventing class. “If I can get a good score in the dressage, we’ll be good to go from there,” Barrett said.

Then there’s Twenty Four Guns, competing in show jumping in what will be his first ever outing.

Barrett’s goal is simple: “Hopefully he can keep a cool head and everything stays calm and he just produces a nice, clear show jump round.”

With several off‑the‑track thoroughbreds in work, Barrett is acutely aware of how critical nutrition is during the transition from racing to equestrian sport. 

“When they are racehorses, they get fed quite a lot of feed,” he explains. “So, when we bring them off the track, we’ve got to establish their diet so that they don’t lose too much condition, and that they stay healthy.”

Jesper uses Pryde’s EasiFeed products across his team.

“We use a lot of the Pryde’s products in what we do. Mostly, the off‑the‑track thoroughbreds go straight onto the Easi Off-the-track and some of them go onto EasiSport as well. We find that really helps them fill out and keep their condition… even put on a fair bit of weight.”

That nutritional support continues right through to competition.

For riders considering an off‑the‑track thoroughbred, Barrett’s advice is simple: patience and basics.

“When you get them off the track… you’ve just got to give them time to adjust to their new environment,” he said. 

“They’re smart animals, they’re quick to learn.”

His approach is slow, steady and structured.

“Just walk, trot, canter around your arena or paddock… make sure they don’t get overwhelmed or overstimulated. Take it day by day, slowly, gradually increasing the workload until you can feel that you can start to produce more from them.”

With a long‑standing commitment to supporting horses through quality nutrition, Pryde’s EasiFeed provides a range of feeds designed to support horses across all stages of their lives and disciplines. As the Official Feed Partner of Equimillion 2026, Pryde’s is on site throughout the weekend, with our Nutrition Team available to offer tailored advice, practical guidance and product support. Riders and spectators are encouraged to visit the Pryde’s team to learn more about setting Thoroughbreds up for success in their second careers.

item.title: Is gut health the missing link in your horse’s overall wellbeing?
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au
item.description: Gut health has become one of the most discussed topics in equine management, and for good reason. The horse’s digestive system is intricate, finely tuned, and responsible for far more than simply breaking down feed. From energy production to immunity and even behaviour, the gut plays a central role in keeping horses healthy, comfortable and performing at their best.
item.content:encoded:
Gut health has become one of the most discussed topics in equine management, and for good reason. The horse’s digestive system is intricate, finely tuned, and responsible for far more than simply breaking down feed. From energy production to immunity and even behaviour, the gut plays a central role in keeping horses healthy, comfortable and performing at their best.

Pryde’s Equine Nutritionist Bethanie Gagliardi says, “When we support the gut, we support the whole horse. A healthy digestive system underpins energy, temperament, immunity and long‑term soundness, it’s one of the most powerful areas owners can influence through feeding and management.”

The horse’s gastrointestinal tract is designed for near‑constant grazing, yet modern feeding routines often challenge this natural system. Knowing how the foregut and hindgut function can help owners make informed decisions that help protect digestive stability and overall health.

Strategies for supporting a healthy equine gut:

 1. Feed according to digestive anatomy

  • The horse’s digestive system is designed for continuous grazing, not large, infrequent meals.

  • Provide  1.5-2% of bodyweight/day (dry matter basis) as forage (pasture and hay).Many horses benefit from 2% or more depending on their individual needs.

  • Maximise chewing time using slow feeders or multiple hay nets.

  • Avoid long periods without forage to reduce stomach acidity and gastric ulcer risk.

2. Prioritise fibre diversity

  • A varied fibre profile supports a stable hindgut microbiome.

  • Mix different hay types.

  • Include high‑fibre feeds such as beet pulp, lupin hulls and chaff.

  • Reduce reliance on high‑starch concentrates.

3. Support foregut function

  • The foregut handles early digestion of protein, fats, starch and sugars.

  • Feed small, frequent meals to avoid overloading the stomach and small intestine.

  • Choose cooked or extruded grains when grains are required.

  • Ensure horses produce saliva by providing regular access to forage.

4. Protect hindgut stability

  • The hindgut is responsible for fibre fermentation, hydration, microbial production of some vitamins (B vitamins and vitamin K) and  emerging research suggests hindgut health may influence behaviour.

  • Introduce new feeds slowly over 14 days.

  • Maintain consistent routines to support microbial balance.

  • Provide constant access to fresh, clean water to aid fermentation and hydration.

 5. Reduce digestive stressors

  • Small management changes can significantly improve gut comfort.

  • Avoid abrupt diet changes.

  • Minimise high‑starch meals.

  • Monitor for early signs of digestive discomfort such as loose manure, irritability or reduced appetite. 

Professional Insight

Gagliardi continues, “Most horses are fed in ways that don’t match how their digestive system works. When owners understand the foregut and hindgut, they can prevent many of the issues we see, from ulcers to behavioural changes. Gut health isn’t just about digestion, it’s about supporting the horse’s entire physiology.”

She emphasises that consistent fibre intake, gradual feed changes and attention to behavioural cues are among the most effective ways to maintain digestive stability.

FAQs

1. What does ‘gut health’ mean in horses?

Gut health refers to the effective functioning of the foregut and hindgut, along with a stable microbial population that supports digestion, nutrient utilisation, immune function and overall wellbeing. 

2. Why is fibre so important?

Fibre fuels hindgut fermentation, producing volatile fatty acids (VFAs) that supply energy, support hydration and contribute to vitamin production.

3. How often should horses eat?

Horses are natural grazers. Long gaps without forage reduce saliva buffering of gastric acid and increase acid exposure in the upper stomach, raising the risk of gastric ulcers.

4. What causes poor gut health?

Common contributors include high‑starch diets, sudden feed changes, low fibre intake, stress, and inconsistent access to forage.

5. How long does digestion take?

The hindgut alone can take 36–72 hours to process fibre, making routine and consistency essential.

6. What are early signs of gut imbalance?

Loose manure, irritability, reduced appetite, weight loss, poor coat or hoof quality, and changes in behaviour may indicate digestive stress.

item.content:encoded:
It’s often that the horses who challenge you, and drive you a little crazy, are the ones that you grow most fond of.

For Pryde’s sponsored rider Elizabeth Welch, or Libby, that’s the case with her beloved mare, Mayfield Frizzante.

Frizzante, like the sparkling water.

Frizzante came into Libby’s life originally arriving as a show jumper for one of her clients. But she quickly showed her personality and power, becoming a little too much for her owner.

Libby’s daughter took to the challenge and fell for Frizzante, riding her all the way through to Grand Prix. Libby rode her during the week, and it was here that her love for Frizzante grew, as she began to understand her better.

“She was challenging. She could be spooky, she could be naughty. But when she was on your team, she was a really great competitor,” Welch said.

Frizzante wasn’t the standout of all the horses Libby has ridden, but she captured her heart more than she thought possible.

When Libby grew more interested in Working Equitation, she thought it would be a great challenge to push Frizzante and see what she was capable of. To Libby's surprise, she took to it “like a duck to water”.

“It was strange because I thought she was going to be naughty and spooky and silly, but it was so amazing to see her engage in working equitation.”

Frizzante reminded Libby of the Lusitano horses from Portugal she adores so much. Horses she believes are full of power and soul. A power which she describes as addictive.

“She was like an ever ready battery, never resting and never waiting. She’s just a keen being.”

That resilience was shaken during a bad storm, when Frizzante got trapped in her stable. As Frizzante began to struggle with her eating, Libby swapped her onto Pryde’s EasiRide and EasiResult to help get her back on track, continuing a relationship that backs much further.

“We’ve been using Pryde’s for 15 years now. I’ve never even had to send a bag back. I’ve found Pryde’s the most consistent. We use such a big variety, but we have a big variety of horses.

For Libby, though, it’s the constant questions about how she gets her horses looking so good that tell her the product works.

“One of the most frequently asked questions we get asked is: How do your horses look so good? And the answer is because we feed Pryde’s.”

These days, Frizzante spends her retirement as the queen of the paddock, mainly because she refuses to share with too many others. Libby visits her 19-year-old mare twice a day to feed her and change her rugs, though the visits still make her emotional.

She’d had so much hope for a big future for Frizzante in working equitation and believed the pair could go far. Unfortunately, Frizzante developed some issues with her hind legs, and her days are now spent in the paddock rather than the arena.

The trait that stands out most about Frizzante is her loyalty. Not to everyone, but unmistakably to her.

“You know, she never really liked that many people in her life, but she’s always come up to me. She’s a very loyal horse.”

It’s that loyalty Libby comes back to when she talks about what Frizzante means to her.

“I always felt like you could go to battle with her and you would probably come out the other end.”

Asked to describe Frizzante in one word, Libby doesn't need to search for an answer. Complicated.

“She’s always been complicated. But I think that's why I like her.”

item.title: How can you keep your horses healthy in persistently wet conditions?
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au
item.description:
With paddocks staying damp and mud lingering long after winter, horse owners are facing ongoing challenges that can impact comfort, hoof health and overall wellbeing.
Pryde’s equine nutritionist Bethanie Gagliardi explains, “Extended wet conditions can be just as stressful for horses as cold weather. The key is staying proactive with daily checks and smart management.”
item.content:encoded:
With paddocks staying damp and mud lingering long after winter, horse owners are facing ongoing challenges that can impact comfort, hoof health and overall wellbeing. 

Pryde’s equine nutritionist Bethanie Gagliardi explains, “Extended wet conditions can be just as stressful for horses as cold weather. The key is staying proactive with daily checks and smart management.”

Here are five essential strategies to help horses stay healthy, dry and thriving through prolonged wet spells.

1. Provide adequate shelter

Even outside of winter, horses need a reliable refuge from rain, wind and soggy ground. A good shelter should:

  • Offer protection from wind and persistent drizzle.

  • Maintain good ventilation to reduce respiratory irritation.

  • Contain dry bedding that’s replaced regularly to prevent dampness.

2. Use waterproof rugs or blankets

Wet coats can quickly lead to chills and discomfort, especially for clipped horses or those who struggle to hold condition:

  • Choose waterproof, breathable rugs to keep horses dry.

  • Check daily for rubbing, shifting or moisture buildup.

  • Remove rugs regularly to inspect skin and coat health.

 3. Maintain hoof health in muddy conditions

Constant moisture increases the risk of thrush, abscesses and soft soles:

  • Pick hooves daily to remove mud and debris.

  • Apply hoof sprays or treatments to prevent bacterial and fungal infections.

  • Rotate turnout areas to avoid deep mud and waterlogged ground.

4. Adjust feeding for higher energy needs

Wet weather can increase energy demands, even when temperatures rise:

  • Provide extra forage such as hay—its digestion naturally generates warmth.

  • Ensure access to fresh, unfrozen water; heated buckets or water warmers help in cooler months.

5. Monitor for stress and early signs of Illness

Persistent wet conditions can affect horses more than owners realise. Watch for:

  • Shivering, lethargy or unexpected weight loss.

  • Wet, matted coats that don’t dry properly.

  • Coughing or nasal discharge that may indicate respiratory issues.

Professional Insight

Pryde’s Equine nutritionist Bethanie Gagliardi adds, “Wet weather management is all about consistency. Small daily habits including checking hooves, monitoring rugs, watching for subtle changes, can prevent bigger health problems before they start.”

FAQs Caring for horses in wet conditions

1. How do I know if my horse’s shelter is suitable for wet weather?

A proper shelter should block wind and rain, offer dry bedding and allow airflow to prevent respiratory irritation.

2. Do horses need rugs when it’s wet but not cold?

Yes - if they’re clipped, underweight, or prone to chills. Waterproof, breathable rugs help keep coats dry and prevent discomfort.

3. Why is hoof care more important during prolonged wet periods?

Mud and moisture create ideal conditions for thrush and abscesses. Daily cleaning and preventative treatments help protect hoof health.

4. Should I increase feed when the weather is wet?

Often, yes. Horses may burn more energy staying warm and comfortable. Extra forage supports both digestion and natural heat production.

5. What signs show my horse is struggling with wet conditions?

Shivering, low energy, weight loss, damp coats and respiratory symptoms all indicate your horse may need additional support.

item.content:encoded:
Every so often, a horse comes along that changes everything. Not because of what they win, but because of what they give back. For Pryde’s sponsored rider Karen Ruzsicska, that horse was her beloved Monty.

Monty, sometimes better known as ‘The Shark’, ‘The Monster’, or just ‘Monster’ for short, was a 14-hand whaler pony from Darwin. He got his nickname from his habit of biting people if they got a little too close. 

“He’d take your finger off in a heartbeat,” Karen said.

Monty was cheeky through and through. He could hear a carrot snap in half from a kilometre away without even turning to look. He rolled his eyes like a teenager and was full of personality. 

Monty was a former riding school pony, who had spent years teaching local kids to jump, play games, and fall in love with horses, which meant by the time Monty became a part of Karen's family, half of Darwin already knew him.

After struggling to find the right horse and feeling a little jaded in the sport she once loved, Karen joked with a friend that she just “needed a Monty.” 

Stars aligned after circumstances changed for Monty’s owner and he found a permanent home with Karen. Four years on, he’d become an unmistakable piece of the family’s heart.

Monty arrived exactly at the right moment, reigniting Karen’s love of show jumping. 

“He was just a really, really fun horse. He just brought the fun back into everything.”

Although Monty would give most things a go, he didn't have that much scope. Karen would take Monty to a few speed classes, some 80cm jumping, and even a little bit of Dressage, although if it were up to Monty, he would rather just eat grass.

Karen had been a loyal Pryde’s feeder long before Monty joined the family. She first fed her horses EasiSport after her niece Olivia Ruzsicska introduced her to the brand, and her loyalty stuck. The results spoke for themselves.

“I have been feeding EasiSport to a number of horses for quite a number of years and I just really liked the result.” 

“Every horse had a brilliant coat, I was able to maintain a steady, feeding ration, and didn't have to adjust too much.”  she said.

Alongside his big personality, Monty also came with a health condition that needed real care. He suffered from Equine Metabolic Syndrome, and his previous owner had already worked hard to manage his weight. Keeping his diet tightly controlled was non-negotiable, and this is where Pryde’s came in.

“I put Monty on EasiSport and EasiFibre as his feed and he stayed on that for the entire time I had him. It did him really well.”

“I just automatically put him on what I had been feeding for years and he looked amazing.”

Monty passed away this last January, and the response caught Karen by surprise. A single post on social media about the loss of her dear Monty, brought comments from people all over Darwin. Former pony club kids, riding school families, anyone who’d ever learned to jump, or been nipped, all expressed how Monty brought joy to them in different ways. 

When suggested that Monty might be something of a local celebrity, Karen laughed. 

“He would have loved being called that.”

item.title: Barrett’s breakthrough: world stage awaits Australia’s rising eventing star
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au
item.description:
Oliver Barrett is ready to take on the world. Having conquered Australia’s top eventing competitions, Barrett earned his selection to the Australian Equestrian Team for the FEI World Equestrian Championships 2026, beginning later this month.
It will be the biggest test yet for the 22-year-old and the moment is not lost on him.
item.content:encoded:
Oliver Barrett is ready to take on the world. Having conquered Australia’s top eventing competitions, Barrett earned his selection to the Australian Equestrian Team for the FEI World Equestrian Championships 2026, beginning later this month.  

It will be the biggest test yet for the 22-year-old and the moment is not lost on him. 

Together with Sandhills Briar, a homebred horse produced by the Barrett family, Oliver will take on the world’s best at Aachen as part of a five strong Australian eventing team.    

Oliver is one of the sport’s most exciting young prospects and his story is only getting started. He finished the end of 2025 as the world number-one U25 eventing rider after topping the FEI Eventing Young Rider Rankings with leading horses Sandhills Briar and Sandhills Special. 

He was selected to ride Briar at the FEI World Equestrian Championships following a standout domestic season, including victories at the Adelaide CCI5* and Sydney CCI4*-L.   

For Oliver, the moment of selection was the culmination of years of hard work.   

“It had been a long buildup and it was something I had my eye on. When we finally got the call, I was excited and all eyes now are on the preparation,” Barrett said.  

The Barrett family are synonymous with Australian eventing. Prue and Craig Barrett, Oliver’s parents, are former Australian representatives and respected elite‑level coaches. Prue and Craig bred Briar at home and have supported Oliver through every stage of his career. 

“I text mum and dad straight away… I could tell from their reply they were very excited… we all got together and we’re all pretty happy. There may have been the odd tear shed.  

 “We have a fair team here at Sandhills… we also have a close connection with Olivia Barton (who was also selected to the team). We were all ecstatic,” he said.   

This will be Oliver’s first time competing in Europe and he is embracing the challenge, hoping the experience feels familiar. 

“I’m really looking forward to it. I think Australians have a pretty good history of coming from Australia and going overseas and being competitive,” he said.   

“Hopefully it’s going to feel like just an ordinary Australian event… I’m still going to have all the same people around me. 

“Eventing is still eventing, still got to do the same thing.”  

Of the horse he’ll share the journey with, Oliver says Briar is up to the challenge.  

“He has a lot of presence… he’s definitely not going to look out of place at all against some of the best horses in the world.”  

Nutrition is a key part of Briar’s preparation, and the Barretts’ long‑standing trust in Pryde’s remains central. When planning Briar’s trip to Europe, Oliver wasn’t willing to compromise.  

“Briar is fed EasiResponse… finding a suitable alternative with the same energy levels overseas proved quite hard. We didn’t want to be changing his main source of energy so Pryde’s feed is making the trip to Aachen with us.”  

“We don’t need to start changing something that’s proven to work exceptionally well for us before a big Championship.” 

With his selection coming at a time when Australia was celebrating two years until the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games and six years until a home Olympics in Brisbane, Oliver knows bigger opportunities lie ahead.  

Right now, Aachen is the focus.  

“This has been the target and now we’re at the target, we’ll be giving it our all to put in our best performance. 

“As soon as Aachen finishes, that’ll be the next goal (LA), as well as Brisbane. We’ve got horses here that mum and dad have bred and that we’re producing. Although many people may not know them now, over the next few years they probably will.” 

The FEI World Equestrian Championships begin on 11 August with the eventing getting underway on Thursday 14 August.

item.title: Pete Comiskey celebrates the next generation as 2026 Gold Buckle Campdraft Championship continues
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au
item.description: The 2026 Gold Buckle Campdraft Championship at Willinga Park marks a special moment for the Comiskey family. For the first time, Peter, the son of Pryde’s sponsored rider Pete Comiskey, will compete in the juvenile class.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Gold Buckle Campdraft Championship at Willinga Park marks a special moment for the Comiskey family. For the first time, Peter, the son of Pryde’s sponsored rider Pete Comiskey, will compete in the juvenile class.

For a family already woven deeply into the sport’s history, it’s an exciting milestone.

“My son Peter is now 13 and he’s going to have a run in the juvenile. He’s very excited to be doing that,” Pete explains.

“With the change around to the calendar this year, with fuel prices the way they were, Willinga was pushed back.

“it’s thrown it into the school holidays so he’s very excited about that… he’s very keen, he’ll be a help with the horses (on the road) and just to see different parts of the country it will be a change of culture for him but it’s all experience that’ll do him a heap of good,” he said.

Pete has spent decades at the top of Australian campdrafting. This year, both he and his wife Bryony have been selected to represent the Australian Campdraft Association in the Pryde’s EasiFeed NCCA National Champion Rider Title at Willinga Park. It’s an honour Pete values deeply.

He and his team arrive at Willinga Park via Clarke Creek in Queensland, where he and Bungarby Elegant Spin won the Open Campdraft at the 2026 Wagyu Crown.

The 2026 Gold Buckle Campdraft Championship incorporating the Pryde’s EasiFeed NCCA Champion Rider title is the second of three major stops, with the Keeroongooloo Cup Campdraft to follow.

“We’ve got three weeks of really good drafting, and we’re really excited about it all,” Pete said prior to their departure.

“We’re right in the middle of our draft here in central Queensland right now,” he explained.

“We had the national finals a couple of weeks ago at Paradise Lagoons.

From Paradise Lagoons to Longreach, Bowen River, Mount Coolon and Nebo, the horses have been working in tough, hot country.

Then comes the shift to New South Wales.

“You go from very warm up here to the very cold down there and the very wet as well.”

The team travelling to Willinga Park is large and experienced. Pete and Bryony each bring five horses, with Jordan McDowell adding three more.

For campdraft fans, the significance of Willinga Park needs little explanation.

“I think it will be a fantastic stage, there’s no better place to ride than Willinga Park,” Pete said.

“It’s a stadium that is nowhere equal to it in Australia. It’s a magnificent stage to ride on.

“The cattle come down from the properties in the Braidwood area, the stock are beautiful cattle and by far (it offers) the biggest prizemoney event.

“There’s nowhere else equal to that in Australia,” he said.

Through all the travel and changing conditions, Pryde’s EasiFeed remains central to Pete’s program.

“The EasiResponse and the EasiOil is a major part of the diet,” he says.

“A lot of the feeds have got the goods in them to help the horses travel and help them recover, to rehydrate… to have that good balanced feed and to keep their system very good.

“We’re proud that Pryde’s continue to keep this national rider title alive. It’s something we find exciting every year to have the best of the best from each association ride. To have an opportunity to ride for your association is a great honour.”

Pryde’s EasiFeed is proud to support the Comiskey’s and all riders striving for excellence at the Pryde’s EasiFeed NCCA National Champion Rider event.

The 2026 Gold Buckle Campdraft Championship begins on 8 July at Willinga Park. More details are available on the event website. Round 1 of the Pryde’s EasiFeed NCCA National Champion Rider begins Thursday at 5pm. Round 2 follows on Friday at 2pm followed by the Final at 4pm on Saturday.

item.description: Willinga Park will be the stage for the Pryde’s EasiFeed NCCA National Champion Rider in 2026, with the prestigious event being held during the Gold Buckle for the first time.
item.content:encoded:
Willinga Park will be the stage for the Pryde’s EasiFeed NCCA National Champion Rider in 2026, with the prestigious event being held during the iconic Gold Buckle Campdraft Championship for the first time.

Already one of Australia’s premier campdrafting showcases, the Championship event brings together elite riders and world‑class horses at a purpose‑built facility for four days of top‑level competition and horsemanship. This year’s program is set to be even more action‑packed with the addition of the Pryde’s EasiFeed NCCA National Champion Rider.

The Pryde’s EasiFeed National Champion Rider features top riders from Australia’s four major Campdrafting Associations - the Gippsland Campdraft Association (GCA), the Australian Bushmen’s Campdraft & Rodeo Association (ABCRA), the Southern Campdrafting Association (SCA) and the Australian Campdraft Association (ACA). Each association will send its best five riders plus its Champion Lady Rider to compete across three rounds. The rider with the highest aggregate score will be crowned the 2026 Pryde’s EasiFeed NCCA National Champion Rider.

Pryde’s Sponsored Rider Mathew Holz is among the elite group of competitors and he’s feeling enthusiastic about returning to Willinga Park.

“It’s such an amazing venue. The facility has been purpose built for campdrafting obviously, so it’s just a great venue,” he said.

Holz’s preparation is well underway, with his horses being brought back into work after a short break. Typically, the NCCA National Champion Rider is held earlier in the year, and the shift in timing has required Holz and his team to adjust their approach.

“Our last competition would have been six or so weeks ago. Normally this is a quiet time of year for us, it’s not in our normal season,” Holz explains.

“We (gave) our horses about a month off after that last competition, and then they’ve been back in (work) for a couple of weeks now. We’re doing all the things that we do to prepare, getting them fit,” Holz said.

A recent training session gave the team a valuable competition‑style tune‑up.

“We were very fortunate to be able to use a private place on the weekend and have a campdraft and give the horses a competition style hit out without being competitive,” he said.

Holz will take seven horses into the event, while his wife Fiona will ride one, with both also contesting Restricted Open and Ladies classes.

He sees the National Champion Rider class as a vital showcase for the sport.

“It’s an event that allows the top riders from each association to compete against one another… it’s a way for all of those people to see who’s top dog on the day,” he said.

Holz is proud to ride under the Pryde’s EasiFeed banner.

“It is an honour to be sponsored by Pryde’s EasiFeed - a brand I’m proud to be associated with and one whose values align closely with my own. In both campdrafting and horse care I believe in doing things with integrity, consistency and a focus on quality and that’s exactly what Prydes delivers to its customers.

“I’ve been lucky enough to compete on some of the best horses in the sport and having them perform at their best has only been possible with the right nutrition behind them. Pryde’s has been part of that journey supporting their health condition and performance through the demands of travel, competition and recovery.”

Pryde’s EasiFeed is proud to support Mathew Holz and all riders striving for excellence at the 2026 Gold Buckle Campdraft Championship and NCCA National Champion Rider event.

item.title: Are You Feeding Your Senior Horse the Right Way?
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au
item.description: Advances in nutrition, veterinary care and management mean horses are living longer than ever before. Many horses remain healthy and active well into their twenties and beyond, but ageing does bring nutritional challenges that require special attention.
item.content:encoded:
Advances in nutrition, veterinary care and management mean horses are living longer than ever before. Many horses remain healthy and active well into their twenties and beyond, but ageing does bring nutritional challenges that require special attention.

Contrary to popular belief, healthy older horses do not automatically lose their ability to digest feed. However, age-related changes such as dental wear, reduced ability to maintain muscle mass, chronic health conditions and altered energy requirements can make meeting nutritional needs more difficult.

Understanding these changes can help owners make informed feeding decisions that support body condition, comfort and quality of life.

What Changes as Horses Age?

Every horse ages differently, but common age-related changes include:

  • Worn, loose or missing teeth

  • Reduced muscle mass

  • Increased risk of PPID (Cushing's disease)

  • Osteoarthritis and chronic pain

  • Changes in appetite or feed intake

  • Greater difficulty maintaining body condition

  • Reduced mobility and altered herd behaviour

These factors often have a greater impact on nutritional status than age itself.

As Pryde's Equine Nutritionist Bethanie Gagliardi explains:

"Many senior horses can continue thriving on well-balanced diets, but early recognition of age-related changes is critical. Small declines in body condition, eating behaviour or muscle mass are often the first signs that a horse's feeding program needs adjustment."

Start With Body Condition

One of the most important indicators of nutritional adequacy in an older horse is body condition. Unexplained weight loss should never be dismissed as a normal consequence of ageing.

Potential causes include:

  • Dental disease

  • Inadequate energy intake

  • Chronic pain

  • Parasitism

  • PPID

  • Poor forage availability

  • Competition from younger horses

  • Underlying illness

Regularly monitoring body condition score and body weight trends can help identify problems before significant weight loss occurs.

Dental Health: The Foundation of Nutrition

Chewing is the first step in digestion.

As horses age, teeth become shorter, wear unevenly and may loosen or be lost completely. Poor dental function reduces chewing efficiency, making it harder to process forage effectively.

Common signs of dental problems include:

  • Weight loss

  • Dropping partially chewed feed (quidding)

  • Slow eating

  • Choke

  • Feed material in manure

  • Bad breath

Routine dental examinations every 6 to 12 months are particularly important for senior horses.

Fibre Remains the Cornerstone

Regardless of age, fibre should remain the foundation of the equine diet.

Most horses should receive a minimum of 1.5-2% of body weight per day as forage (dry matter basis), with many benefiting from 2% or more depending on their individual needs, workload and body condition.

Suitable fibre sources include:

  • Pasture

  • Grass hay

  • Lucerne hay

  • Chaff

  • Soaked hay cubes

  • Beet pulp

  • Lupin hulls

  • Copra meal

  • High-fibre pelleted feeds

Maintaining adequate fibre intake supports digestive health, encourages chewing and helps maintain hindgut function.

Supporting Horses With Dental Challenges

The goal is not necessarily to remove forage, but to ensure fibre requirements continue to be met using forms the horse can comfortably consume.

For horses with mild dental issues:

  • Use softer, leafy hays

  • Increase chaff intake

  • Include highly digestible fibre sources

  • Feed nutrient-dense feeds such as Pryde’s OldTimer or EasiConditioner where appropriate

For horses with severe dental compromise:

  • Replace some or all long-stem forage with:

    • Soaked hay cubes

    • Soaked beet pulp

    • Fibre pellets such as EasiFibre

    • Complete senior feeds

    • Soft fibre mashes

  • Provide a nutrient dense soakable feed such as Pryde’s EasiConditioner or BioMare Cubes.

These alternatives can help maintain fibre intake without compromising chewing comfort.

Protein Becomes Increasingly Important              

One of the most significant nutritional changes associated with ageing is a reduced ability to maintain muscle mass.

Older horses often benefit from diets containing high-quality protein sources rich in essential amino acids.

Good protein sources include:

  • Lucerne

  • Soybean meal

  • Quality commercial senior feeds

  • Lupins

Maintaining adequate protein intake supports topline, muscle condition and overall functionality.

When evaluating senior horses, loss of muscle mass may be a more important indicator than body weight alone.

Managing PPID and Metabolic Concerns

Senior horses have a higher incidence of Pituitary Pars Intermedia Dysfunction (PPID), commonly known as Cushing's disease. Some older horses may also develop insulin dysregulation, increasing the risk of laminitis.

For these horses:

  • Prioritise low NSC forage sources (<10% NSC)

  • Limit access to high-sugar pasture when necessary

  • Consider soaking hay where appropriate

  • Choose low-starch, high-fibre feeds such as Pryde’s EasiSport

  • Work closely with a veterinarian to monitor the condition

Nutritional management should always be based on the individual horse rather than age alone.

Every Senior Horse Is Different

There is no single feeding program that suits every older horse.

A successful senior nutrition plan should consider:

  • Dental health

  • Body condition

  • Muscle mass

  • Activity level

  • Forage intake

  • Medical conditions

  • Social environment

Regular assessment and early intervention are often the key factors that allow horses to remain healthy and comfortable throughout their later years.

Professional Insight

Bethanie Gagliardi says:

"One of the biggest misconceptions about senior horses is that ageing automatically causes poor digestion. While some horses require dietary modifications, factors such as dental health, muscle maintenance, chronic disease and overall management often have a much greater influence on nutritional status than age alone."

FAQs

Do older horses digest fibre less efficiently?

Healthy older horses often maintain fibre digestion comparable to younger adult horses. However, dental problems, disease and reduced feed intake can compromise overall nutritional status.

Why do senior horses lose muscle?

Age-related muscle loss is common and may be influenced by reduced activity, inadequate protein intake, chronic disease or PPID.

How often should senior horses receive dental care?

Most senior horses should receive a dental examination every 6 to 12 months.

What is the best fibre source for older horses?

The best choice depends on dental function, but pasture, hay, chaff, beet pulp, soaked hay cubes and other highly digestible fibre sources are commonly used.

Should all senior horses receive a senior feed?

Not necessarily. Many senior horses maintain condition well on standard feeding programs. Diet changes should be based on individual needs rather than age alone.

What's the most important thing to monitor?

Body condition, muscle mass, dental health and changes in eating behaviour are among the most valuable indicators of nutritional wellbeing.

item.title: Why do some horses refuse their feed and what you can do about it
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au
item.description: Getting a fussy eater to eat is no easy task, especially when a horse suddenly refuses its usual ration. “A horse’s appetite is one of the most important indicators of digestive comfort. When a horse becomes selective or stops eating, it’s often their way of telling us something isn’t quite right,” says Pryde’s in‑house nutritionist, Bethanie Gagliardi.
item.content:encoded:
Getting a fussy eater to eat is no easy task, especially when a horse suddenly refuses its usual ration.  

“A horse’s appetite is one of the most important indicators of digestive comfort. When a horse becomes selective or stops eating, it’s often their way of telling us something isn’t quite right,” says Pryde’s in‑house nutritionist, Bethanie Gagliardi.

To help owners navigate this frustrating challenge, The Pryde’s nutrition team has outlined practical strategies proven to encourage even the pickiest horses to eat consistently.

Key strategies to support a fussy eater

1. Remove salt and electrolytes temporarily

Salt can make feed less appealing when a horse already has a reduced appetite. Removing it for a short period can help restore interest in the feed.

2. Choose cooked grains or non‑grain feeds

Uncooked grains can push starch into the hindgut, reducing appetite. Cooked grains and fibre‑based feeds support healthy fermentation and vitamin B1 production, an essential appetite stimulant.

3. Feed a ration that tastes genuinely good

Highly palatable, fully fortified complete feeds reduce the need for unnecessary supplements and encourage horses to eat willingly.

4. Avoid diet changes at competitions or events

Stress and unfamiliar environments already challenge appetite. Introducing new feeds or supplements at events can make meals even less appealing.

Pryde’s EasiResult and EasiPerformance are both formulated with palatability in mind, making them ideal options for horses who regularly turn their nose up at their feed.

Professional Insight

Pryde’s Equine nutritionist Bethanie Gagliardi explains, “When a horse becomes fussy, our priority is to reduce anything that may be affecting flavour or digestive comfort. Small adjustments can make a big difference to appetite and overall wellbeing.”

FAQs About feeding fussy horses

1. Why should I remove salt from my horse’s feed if they stop eating?

Salt can intensify flavours and make feed less appealing when appetite is already low. Removing it temporarily helps reset taste preferences before gradually reintroducing it.

2. Do cooked grains really help with appetite?

Yes. Cooked grains prevent excess starch from entering the hindgut, supporting healthy fibre fermentation and vitamin B1 production, both essential for maintaining appetite.

3. Is it better to keep the diet simple for picky eaters?

Absolutely. Over‑supplementing can make feed unpalatable. A complete, fortified feed paired with forage is often the most effective approach.

4. Why do horses go off their feed at events?

Stress, travel, and unfamiliar surroundings can disrupt eating habits. Keeping the diet consistent and allowing plenty of grazing time helps maintain appetite.

5. Which Pryde’s feeds suit fussy eaters?

EasiResult and EasiPerformance are specifically designed to be highly palatable and nutritionally balanced for horses that are selective or inconsistent eaters.

For riders across Australia, the Melbourne International Three Day Event is widely regarded as a milestone competition. An iconic event that attracts competitors of all ages and stages of their careers.

 

For Tasmania’s Ruby Hirst, proudly supported by Pryde’s EasiFeed, the 2026 event marked the fulfilment of a dream she had carried for many years.

 

Ruby is part of the well‑known Hirst family, whose connection to Pryde’s spans her sisters, Alice and Bethany, who have been sponsored by Pryde’s for many years.

 

Ruby had previously qualified for Melbourne in 2024 but was forced to withdraw due to injury. Returning in 2026 was therefore a significant personal achievement, made even more remarkable given the challenges she faced in the lead‑up.

 

“It’s just been such a big goal of mine for so many years… I’ve always wanted to be at Melbourne,” Hirst said.

 

“Competing there was honestly incredible.”

 

Just two weeks before the event, Ruby suffered a serious wrist injury, leaving her with limited preparation time. With the help of friends who kept her horses in work, she managed one ride before loading them for the journey across Bass Strait.

 

“As long as I got there and tried my best was my only thought,” she said.

 

Competing in the CCN1*, Ruby campaigned two Off‑The‑Track Thoroughbreds she has trained herself - Speedy Sky and Katzenjammer. Speedy Sky delivered a clear cross‑country round and finished 16th, while both horses handled the atmosphere with maturity.

 

While Melbourne is a major undertaking for any rider, Ruby’s journey is particularly unique. Unlike most competitors, her preparation involves navigating an ocean crossing.

 

“I take a 12‑hour boat ride with the horses where they stay in the float… and then I get off the boat, give them a rest and make my journey to whatever event I’m going to.”

 

Based near Launceston, Ruby travels an hour to Devonport before boarding the boat. Once in Victoria, the trip to Werribee is short, but the Bass Strait crossing requires careful planning - especially when travelling with sensitive Thoroughbreds.

 

“We’re not allowed to feed them on the boat… so it’s making sure I actually do really good prep before and after the event because the boat trip can strip the weight off them,” Ruby explained.

 

“I went to Ballarat a month ago and I came home expecting them to be a bit more light on, and they honestly looked the best they’ve every looked, because of the prep,” she said.    

 

For her Melbourne campaign, Ruby fed EasiConditioner, adding LupinPak when her horses needed additional support.

 

“My horses perform well on Pryde’s… they look fantastic on Pryde’s.”

 

Pryde’s EasiFeed is proud to support the Melbourne International Three Day Event and all riders who take on this iconic competition, including dedicated and determined athletes like Ruby, who represent the next generation shaping the future of Australian eventing.

item.content:encoded:
Few weekends on the Australian eventing calendar carry the same sense of tradition as the Melbourne International Three Day Event.

 

Each June long weekend, Werribee Park becomes a hub of world‑class sport, drawing big crowds who line the cross-country course and fill the stands for dressage and show jumping. It’s an event riders mark on their calendars year after year and one that blends history and prestige with a winter buzz that only Melbourne can deliver.

 

This year’s edition once again promises depth, quality and a fiercely contested top class. The premier class, the Pryde’s EasiFeed CCI4*-L has attracted a strong field of established names and rising combinations, all looking to make their mark on one of Australia’s most popular and iconic three‑day events.

 

Among them is Queensland’s Matt Gaske, returning to Melbourne for the first time in seven years and stepping up with Leads the Way for the horse’s debut at this level. For Gaske, simply being back at Werribee is something special.

 

“I’m super excited about going down there,” Gaske said. “It’s somewhere we always aim to be at every year. And to have a horse at that level again is exciting,” he said.

 

The pair arrive off the back of a confident preparation, including recent runs at Fig Tree Pocket and solid show jumping form.

 

While this is Leads the Way’s first CCI4* start, Gaske feels the horse is ready for the challenge.

 

“He’s very consistent at the 3 stars, so I think he’s all set and well prepped to be doing the 4 star this weekend at Melbourne,” he said.

 

For Gaske, Melbourne is also a stepping stone toward a bigger ambition…. Adelaide.

 

“I went to Adelaide in April just with my daughter, and I made a bit of a pact with myself and went, well, I want to get to Adelaide this time next year, and to get there, I set myself some short-term long-term goals, and this is one of those that I have to tick off,” he said.

 

And while Leads the Way may not be the most conventional type, Gaske believes the gelding has the heart and grit to go far.

 

“He’s obviously green at four star… but he doesn’t want to touch the rail, so he is careful but he does go a little bit his own way

“I think that he could be a 5 star horse… he’s giving me all the answers that he wants to be so at this stage, that’s what we’re aiming him for.”

 

As for the long‑term dream - Brisbane 2032 and a home Olympic Games, virtually in his backyard - Gaske is realistic but optimistic.

 

“I think it crosses everyone’s mind that does eventing.

 

“He’ll definitely have the experience to be there… at the end of the day… it’s about the heart. And for this horse… he’s got the heart to be a warrior.”

 

Pryde’s EasiFeed proudly supporting the CCI4*-L

 

Pryde’s EasiFeed is pleased to once again support the Melbourne International Three Day Event, sponsoring the feature CCI4*-L class and backing the riders and horses who make this weekend such a highlight of the season.

 

For Gaske, Pryde’s plays a crucial role in preparing his team, especially when travelling from Queensland to Victoria.

 

“With Pryde’s it starts months in advance. Prepping the horses to be in the best performance quality that we can have them in… we increase their feeds a little bit more, knowing that they’ll be traveling down there… and then once they are there it’s keeping the consistency and quality of the feed.”

 

That consistency, he says, is key to keeping horses settled, strong and ready to perform.

 

“It’s a familiarity that they can be comfortable in… and we increase their feeds with giving them a little bit more of an energy intake the day before cross-country. Pryde’s are very supportive in all the different style feeds that they do feed… and each horse, we tailor a different feed to.”

 

As the action unfolds at Werribee, the CCI4*-L promises to be a showcase of talent, and partnership - qualities Pryde’s EasiFeed is proud to champion.

item.title: Feeding the ageing horse in winter: how to keep weight on when the weather turns cold
item.dc:creator: kylieh@prydes.com.au

item.content:encoded:
As temperatures drop and pasture availability decreases, many older horses begin to struggle with maintaining condition. Winter can be especially tough on ageing digestive systems, reduced chewing ability, and horses who simply don’t regulate body temperature as efficiently as they once did.

One of the biggest challenges we see in senior horses during winter a decrease in body condition and muscling and topline” explains Pryde’s resident expert, equine nutritionist Bethanie Gagliardi.

“Older horses often need more support to maintain condition, so choosing fibre sources and supplementary feeds that are highly digestible becomes essential as the weather cools.”

Here are four practical strategies from our expert nutritionist team to help your older horse stay healthy, comfortable, and in good condition all winter long.

1. Prioritise forage - and make it easy to chew

Forage should always form the foundation of your horse’s diet, but it becomes even more important in winter when pasture availability drops. Long‑stem hay is ideal, but many older horses struggle to chew it effectively due to dental wear or missing teeth.

If that’s the case, consider incorporating softer, more digestible fibre sources such as hay cubes, chaff or fibre‑based pellets like EasiFibre. These options provide the gut‑friendly fibre your horse needs while reducing the risk of choke or undigested feed passing through the system.

2. Add a high‑quality supplementary feed for weight gain

Senior horses often need more digestible energy and quality protein than forage alone can provide. A well‑balanced supplementary feed can make all the difference in maintaining weight through winter.

Feeds such as OldTimer or EasiConditioner offer slow‑release energy, quality protein, and essential nutrients tailored to support older horses. These feeds help promote steady weight gain, maintain topline, and support overall vitality - without creating fizzy behaviour.

3. Rug strategically to reduce energy loss

Older horses can burn a surprising amount of energy simply trying to stay warm. Rugging can help reduce this energy drain, especially during cold, wet, or windy weather.

A well‑fitted, waterproof, insulated rug helps your horse conserve body heat, meaning more of their dietary energy can go toward maintaining weight rather than fighting the elements. Just remember to check rugs daily for fit, rubbing, and cleanliness.

4. Stay on top of health checks and preventative care

Even the best feeding plan won’t be effective if underlying health issues are at play. Weight loss in older horses is often linked to dental problems, parasite burdens, or unmanaged pain.

Before winter sets in, make sure your senior horse is:

  • Up to date with their de‑worming program

  • Receiving regular dental checks

  • Assessed for any age‑related pain, such as arthritis, that may affect appetite or mobility

  • A healthy horse is far better equipped to maintain condition through the colder months.

Set your older horse up for a healthy winter

Winter doesn’t have to mean weight loss for your ageing horse. With the right combination of digestible fibre, supportive supplementary feeds, thoughtful rugging, and proactive health care, you can help them stay comfortable, strong, and in great condition all season long.

If you’d like personalised feeding advice for your senior horse, our Pryde’s EasiFeed [KH1] selector found on our website can help.

 

Frequently Asked Question

Q. Should I feed more protein to an older horse? – Yes

Older horses often struggle to maintain muscle and topline. Providing high‑quality, easily digestible protein helps support muscle maintenance, immune function, and overall condition. Senior feeds such as OldTimer or EasiConditioner are designed to deliver this high quality protein, in the amounts aged horses require,

Q. Should I rug an older horse in winter? – Yes

Ageing horses burn more energy trying to stay warm, especially in cold, wet, or windy weather. Rugging helps reduce this energy loss by conserving body heat, allowing more of their dietary energy to go toward maintaining weight and condition. A well‑fitted, waterproof rug can make a significant difference, particularly for horses with reduced ability to regulate body temperature.

Q. Should I change my horse’s diet in winter? – Yes

Winter brings reduced pasture availability and increased energy demands, so most older horses benefit from dietary adjustments. This often includes:

Increased forage provision in the form of digestible fibre sources (e.g., hay cubes, chaff, soaked fibre pellets) if chewing long‑stem hay is difficult.

A senior‑appropriate supplementary feed to support weight gain and vitality

Monitoring and adjusting feed quantities as temperatures drop.

These changes help ensure your horse receives enough energy, fibre, and nutrients to stay healthy and maintain condition throughout the colder months.
